$comment: Honour India seed dataset. Each record honours one Indian scientist or great mind. Fields: slug (stable id), name, born/died (year, died null if living), field, tagline (one line shown on billboards), summary (2-3 sentences), quote (only where widely attributed; null otherwise), wiki (exact English Wikipedia page title, used to fetch the portrait and build the link). Image credit/license live in data/images.json, produced by scripts/fetch-images.mjs.

figures.name: C. V. Raman
figures.tagline: Discovered how light shifts colour as it scatters — the Raman effect — winning India its first Nobel Prize in the sciences.
figures.summary: Raman found that when light passes through a transparent substance, a tiny fraction emerges with a shifted wavelength — the Raman effect, announced on 28 February 1928. The discovery won him the 1930 Nobel Prize in Physics, and India now celebrates National Science Day on its anniversary. He founded the Raman Research Institute and received the Bharat Ratna in 1954.

quote.text: The true wealth of a nation consists not in the stored-up gold but in the intellectual and physical strength of its people.

figures.name: Srinivasa Ramanujan
figures.tagline: Self-taught genius whose identities in number theory still guide mathematics a century after his death.
figures.summary: With almost no formal training in pure mathematics, Ramanujan produced thousands of results in number theory, infinite series and continued fractions. His 1913 letters to G. H. Hardy brought him to Cambridge, where he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society at thirty. His notebooks continue to yield new mathematics to this day.

quote.text: An equation for me has no meaning unless it expresses a thought of God.
quote.source: as recounted in accounts of his life

figures.name: Jagadish Chandra Bose
figures.tagline: Demonstrated wireless signalling in 1895, then proved that plants respond to stimuli — a pioneer of two sciences.
figures.summary: In 1895 in Calcutta, Bose publicly demonstrated communication using millimetre-range radio waves, before Marconi's wireless patent. He then turned to plant physiology, inventing the crescograph to measure how plants respond to light, heat and gravity, and founded the Bose Institute in 1917. He rarely patented his inventions, believing knowledge should be free.

figures.name: Homi J. Bhabha
figures.tagline: Architect of India's atomic energy programme and founder of the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research.
figures.summary: A physicist of international standing in cosmic rays and quantum theory, Bhabha founded the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research in 1945 and became the first chairman of India's Atomic Energy Commission. He charted the country's three-stage nuclear power programme and mentored a generation of Indian scientists before dying in an air crash on Mont Blanc.

figures.name: Satyendra Nath Bose
figures.tagline: His way of counting photons forced physics to invent new statistics — the bosons carry his name.
figures.summary: In 1924 Bose sent Albert Einstein a paper deriving Planck's radiation law in a way that treated light as indistinguishable quanta. Einstein translated and extended it, and Bose–Einstein statistics — and much later the Bose–Einstein condensate — were born. Particles obeying his statistics are called bosons. India later honoured him as National Professor with the Padma Vibhushan.

figures.name: Meghnad Saha
figures.tagline: Derived the equation that lets astronomers take the temperature of stars from their light.
figures.summary: Saha's 1920 ionization equation connects a star's spectrum to its temperature and pressure — the foundation of modern astrophysics. He also built institutions: the journal Science and Culture, and what is now the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics in Kolkata. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1927.

figures.name: S. Chandrasekhar
figures.tagline: Worked out how stars die — the Chandrasekhar limit names the tipping point beyond which they collapse.
figures.summary: At nineteen, on the ship from India to Cambridge, Chandrasekhar calculated that white dwarf stars cannot exceed about 1.4 solar masses. The idea was resisted for decades and finally earned the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics. NASA named its flagship X-ray observatory, Chandra, after him.

figures.name: Vikram Sarabhai
figures.tagline: Father of the Indian space programme — from a rocket shed in Kerala to India's first satellite.
figures.summary: Sarabhai convinced a young India that space technology could serve development — communication, weather forecasting and education. He founded the Physical Research Laboratory, led the committee that grew into ISRO, and set up the Thumba launching station where India's first rockets were assembled beside a fishing village. He also helped found IIM Ahmedabad.

quote.text: We must be second to none in the application of advanced technologies to the real problems of man and society.
quote.source: on the purpose of India's space programme

figures.name: A. P. J. Abdul Kalam
figures.tagline: The 'Missile Man' who led India's rocket and missile programmes, then became its most beloved President.
figures.summary: An aeronautical engineer who helped build India's first satellite launcher, SLV-3, and led the integrated guided missile programme that produced Agni and Prithvi — earning the name 'Missile Man of India'. As the eleventh President (2002–2007) he became the 'People's President', and spent his last decades inspiring students. He died while delivering a lecture, at eighty-three.

quote.text: Dream is not that which you see while sleeping; it is something that does not let you sleep.

figures.name: M. S. Swaminathan
figures.tagline: Plant geneticist who helped end India's food dependence — the architect of the Green Revolution.
figures.summary: Combining high-yielding wheat varieties with strategy and farmer outreach, Swaminathan helped turn India from a food-deficient nation into one self-sufficient in grain within a decade of the mid-1960s crises. He later founded the M. S. Swaminathan Research Foundation and championed an 'evergreen revolution' — productivity that respects ecology. He was the first laureate of the World Food Prize, in 1987.

figures.name: Verghese Kurien
figures.tagline: The 'Milkman of India' — built Operation Flood and the cooperative movement that made India the world's largest milk producer.
figures.summary: An engineer who planned to leave for a petroleum career, Kurien stayed in Anand, Gujarat, and built Amul into a farmer-owned dairy cooperative. Replicating that model through Operation Flood, he made India the world's largest milk producer, with millions of small farmers as its owners.

figures.name: Anna Mani
figures.tagline: Insisted India build its own weather instruments — the 'weather woman of India'.
figures.summary: Trained as a physicist, Mani made her mark in meteorological instrumentation, insisting that India manufacture its scientific instruments rather than import them. As deputy director general of the India Meteorological Department she built networks for measuring solar radiation, ozone and wind — foundations for India's renewable-energy planning. A 2022 Google Doodle celebrated her 104th birthday.
figures.commonsFile: Anna Mani - Oil painting by Rajasekharan.jpg

figures.name: E. K. Janaki Ammal
figures.tagline: Bred sweeter sugarcane for India and co-authored the Chromosome Atlas of Cultivated Plants.
figures.summary: Earning a doctorate in botany in Michigan in 1931, Janaki Ammal became a leading cytogeneticist, crossing sugarcane varieties to give India sweeter, hardier canes. She co-authored the Chromosome Atlas of Cultivated Plants, helped reorganise the Botanical Survey of India, and received the Padma Shri in 1977. A magnolia — Magnolia 'Janaki Ammal' — is named in her honour.

figures.name: Asima Chatterjee
figures.tagline: Pioneered medicines from Indian plants — the first woman to earn a DSc from an Indian university.
figures.summary: Chatterjee's research on alkaloids from Indian plants led to anti-convulsive and anti-malarial compounds, including the anti-epileptic drug Ayush-56. In 1944 she became the first woman awarded a Doctorate of Science by an Indian university, and in 1975 the first woman to preside over the Indian Science Congress.
figures.imageNote: No freely-licensed portrait is available yet; the widget shows a monogram until one is contributed.

figures.name: Anandi Gopal Joshi
figures.tagline: One of the first Indian women doctors, graduating in medicine in America in 1886 — at twenty-one.
figures.summary: Sent to America with her husband's support, Joshi graduated from the Women's Medical College of Pennsylvania in 1886, among the first Indian women to qualify in Western medicine. Queen Victoria sent her a congratulatory message. She died of tuberculosis within a year of returning home, before her work could begin.

figures.name: Kadambini Ganguly
figures.tagline: One of British India's first women doctors — in practice when women could hardly leave the home.
figures.summary: Ganguly was among the first women graduates of Calcutta University and, in 1886, among the first women of South Asia to qualify as a doctor of Western medicine. She practised for decades, worked for women's education and rights, and was among the first women to speak at the Indian National Congress.

figures.name: G. N. Ramachandran
figures.tagline: Mapped the shapes a protein chain can fold into — the Ramachandran plot is in every textbook since.
figures.summary: In 1963 Ramachandran and his students plotted the full range of angles a protein backbone can adopt, creating the Ramachandran plot — still the first check on any new protein structure. A decade earlier he had proposed the triple-helix structure of collagen. He built India's leading school of molecular biophysics in Chennai.
figures.imageNote: No freely-licensed portrait is available yet; the widget shows a monogram until one is contributed.

figures.name: Yellapragada Subbarow
figures.tagline: Co-discovered how ATP carries the cell's energy, and developed lifesaving drugs — one of science's most unsung minds.
figures.summary: At Harvard, Subbarow and Cyrus Fiske isolated ATP and phosphocreatine, the molecules that store and carry energy in every living cell. Moving to Lederle Laboratories, he drove the development of diethylcarbamazine against filariasis, methotrexate against cancer, and the tetracycline antibiotics. A colleague's memorial line: 'Because he lived, the world lives.'

figures.name: Birbal Sahni
figures.tagline: Read plant fossils hundreds of millions of years old to reconstruct the Indian subcontinent's deep past.
figures.summary: Sahni founded palaeobotany as a discipline in India, studying fossils from the Gondwana deposits to trace the subcontinent's ancient vegetation. The institute he established in Lucknow, now the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences, carries the work forward. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1936.

figures.name: P. C. Mahalanobis
figures.tagline: Founded the Indian Statistical Institute and the measure that bears his name — the Mahalanobis distance.
figures.summary: Mahalanobis started the Indian Statistical Institute in 1931 with a few students in a Calcutta classroom and built it into a world centre. He created the Mahalanobis distance, pioneered large-scale sample surveys, and brought statistics to national planning. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 1968.

figures.name: Sálim Ali
figures.tagline: The 'Birdman of India' — surveyed the subcontinent's birds and made citizens into naturalists.
figures.summary: Ali surveyed the birds of the subcontinent across decades of expeditions, from the Himalaya to the Andamans, and wrote The Book of Indian Birds, which turned generations of readers into observers. With Dillon Ripley he produced the landmark Handbook of the Birds of India and Pakistan. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 1976.

figures.name: Shakuntala Devi
figures.tagline: The 'human computer' — multiplied two 13-digit numbers in 28 seconds, and made numbers fun for millions.
figures.summary: Discovered as a child prodigy in Bangalore, Devi performed calculations that outran computers of her era — in 1982 she multiplied two randomly chosen 13-digit numbers in 28 seconds. She wrote books bringing mathematics to children, and in 1977 wrote the first Indian study of homosexuality, arguing for its decriminalisation.

figures.name: M. Visvesvaraya
figures.tagline: Engineer of dams and water systems — India celebrates Engineers' Day on his birthday.
figures.summary: Visvesvaraya patented automatic sluice gates, engineered the Krishna Raja Sagara dam and city water and drainage systems, and as Diwan of Mysore industrialised the state. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1955, and India marks Engineers' Day on his birthday, 15 September.

quote.text: Remember, your work may be only to sweep a railway crossing, but it is your duty to keep it so clean that no other crossing in the world is as clean as yours.

figures.name: Kalpana Chawla
figures.tagline: First woman of Indian origin in space — flew twice on the Space Shuttle.
figures.summary: Born in Karnal, Haryana, Chawla earned her doctorate in aerospace engineering in the United States and was selected by NASA in 1994. She flew on Space Shuttle Columbia in 1997, operating the robotic arm, and again on STS-107 in 2003 — the mission that ended in tragedy on re-entry. Asteroid 51826 Kalpanachawla and NASA's Kalpana Chawla supercomputer bear her name.

quote.text: The path from dreams to success does exist. May you have the vision to find it, the courage to get on to it, and the perseverance for the journey.
quote.source: widely quoted from her message to students

figures.name: Nambi Narayanan
figures.tagline: Led development of the Vikas engine that still powers Indian rockets — and fought a false case to vindication.
figures.summary: At ISRO, Narayanan led the team that developed the Vikas liquid engine — the workhorse of the PSLV and GSLV rockets. In 1994 he was arrested in a fabricated espionage case; the charges collapsed, and decades later the Supreme Court upheld his innocence and India awarded him the Padma Bhushan in 2019.

figures.name: Tessy Thomas
figures.tagline: First woman to head a major Indian missile project — led Agni-IV as its project director.
figures.summary: Joining DRDO in 1985, Thomas rose through the Agni programme to become project director of Agni-IV — the first woman to lead a major Indian missile project — and later directed the Advanced Systems Laboratory. Known as the 'Missile Woman of India', she has championed women in engineering throughout her career.

figures.name: G. D. Naidu
figures.tagline: Self-taught inventor called the 'Edison of India' — built motors, pumps and cameras from scratch.
figures.summary: With little formal schooling, Naidu built one of India's earliest indigenous electric motors, manufactured the Rasant razor, pumps and film cameras, and ran Coimbatore's famous industrial exhibition. He later endowed a polytechnic and a museum of technology, seeding the engineering culture of his city.
figures.imageNote: No freely-licensed portrait is available yet; the widget shows a monogram until one is contributed.

figures.name: Raj Chandra Bose
figures.tagline: Co-created the BCH error-correcting codes that keep modern digital storage and communication honest.
figures.summary: Rising from poverty in Mymensingh to the heart of Calcutta statistics, Bose co-constructed the BCH error-correcting codes with his student D. K. Ray-Chaudhuri in 1959–60 — mathematics that underpins reliable digital storage and communication today. He also developed foundational tools of combinatorial design, including the Bose–Mesner algebra, and spent his final decades building a combinatorics school in Colorado.
figures.imageNote: No freely-licensed portrait is available yet; the widget shows a monogram until one is contributed.

figures.name: Prafulla Chandra Ray
figures.tagline: Father of Indian chemistry — founded Bengal Chemicals, India's first pharmaceutical company.
figures.summary: P. C. Ray was a pioneering chemist who established modern chemical research in India. He discovered mercurous nitrite in 1896 and founded Bengal Chemicals & Pharmaceutical Works in 1901, India's first pharmaceutical company, proving Indian industry could manufacture medicines. He authored the seminal 'History of Hindu Chemistry' and mentored generations of Indian chemists.

figures.name: E. C. George Sudarshan
figures.tagline: Theoretical physicist who co-originated the V–A theory of weak interactions and the Sudarshan–Glauber representation in quantum optics.
figures.summary: Sudarshan made foundational contributions to quantum optics and particle physics. With Robert Marshak he proposed the V–A (vector minus axial vector) structure of weak interactions in 1957, a key insight behind the Standard Model. His Sudarshan–Glauber representation is a cornerstone of quantum optics, and he also explored the quantum Zeno effect and tachyons. He taught at the University of Texas and the Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Chennai.

figures.name: Jayant V. Narlikar
figures.tagline: Cosmologist who co-developed the Hoyle–Narlikar theory of gravity and made steady-state cosmology a serious alternative to the Big Bang.
figures.summary: Narlikar is an eminent cosmologist known for his work on steady-state cosmology and the Hoyle–Narlikar theory, a conformal theory of gravity developed with Fred Hoyle. He founded the Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (IUCAA) in Pune and has written extensively to popularize science in India and abroad. A recipient of the Padma Vibhushan and Padma Bhushan.

figures.name: Roddam Narasimha
figures.tagline: Pioneer of fluid dynamics and aerospace research in India — studied atmospheric turbulence and led NAL.
figures.summary: Narasimha was a leading aerospace scientist and fluid dynamicist who made fundamental contributions to the study of turbulence, atmospheric flows, and aircraft design. He served as Director of the National Aerospace Laboratories (NAL), Bangalore, and was a professor at IISc and IIT Kanpur. He played a key role in building India's aerospace research infrastructure and received the Padma Vibhushan.

figures.name: Bikash Sinha
figures.tagline: Nuclear physicist who led India's participation in CERN experiments and directed the Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre.
figures.summary: Sinha was a nuclear physicist who established high-energy nuclear physics research in India and led India's collaboration with CERN, including work on the ALICE experiment studying quark-gluon plasma. He directed the Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC), Kolkata, and the Saha Institute of Nuclear Physics. A Padma Bhushan recipient, he worked to connect Indian science with global particle physics.

figures.name: Satish Dhawan
figures.tagline: Father of experimental fluid dynamics research in India and third chairman of ISRO — guided India's early space programme.
figures.summary: Dhawan was an aerospace engineer who founded India's first supersonic wind tunnel at IISc Bangalore and established a school of fluid dynamics research. As ISRO chairman from 1972 to 1984, he oversaw the development of India's satellite launch capability, including the SLV-3 and the early PSLV. The Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota is named in his honour. He received the Padma Vibhushan.

figures.name: Udupi Ramachandra Rao
figures.tagline: Space scientist who led the development of India's first satellite, Aryabhata, and served as ISRO chairman.
figures.summary: U. R. Rao was a space scientist who shaped India's space programme from its early days. He led the team that built Aryabhata, India's first satellite (launched 1975), and directed the development of several subsequent satellites. As ISRO chairman (1984–1994), he oversaw the operational PSLV and the beginnings of India's remote-sensing and communications satellite constellations. He received the Padma Vibhushan and was inducted into the Satellite Hall of Fame.

figures.name: K. Kasturirangan
figures.tagline: ISRO chairman who oversaw the operational PSLV and GSLV and India's first lunar mission, Chandrayaan-1.
figures.summary: Kasturirangan was an astrophysicist and ISRO chairman (1994–2003) during a transformative period. Under his leadership India achieved operational capability with the PSLV and GSLV launch vehicles, and launched Chandrayaan-1, India's first mission to the Moon. He later served as a Member of the Planning Commission and Chancellor of several universities. A Padma Vibhushan recipient.

figures.name: G. Madhavan Nair
figures.tagline: ISRO chairman who led Chandrayaan-1 to the Moon and operationalized the GSLV and PSLV launch programmes.
figures.summary: Nair was an aerospace engineer and ISRO chairman (2003–2009) who guided Chandrayaan-1, which confirmed water molecules on the lunar surface. He oversaw successful operational flights of PSLV and GSLV and expansion of India's INSAT and IRS satellite systems. A Padma Vibhushan recipient and former chairman of the board of governors of IIT Bombay.

figures.name: A. S. Kiran Kumar
figures.tagline: ISRO chairman during the Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) — India's first interplanetary probe.
figures.summary: Kiran Kumar was a scientist-engineer who developed electro-optical sensors for India's remote-sensing satellites and served as ISRO chairman (2015–2018). During his tenure ISRO successfully launched the Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan), making India the first Asian nation to reach Mars orbit and the first in the world to do so on its first attempt. He received the Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan.

figures.name: K. Sivan
figures.tagline: ISRO chairman known as the 'Rocket Man' — led Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3 lunar missions.
figures.summary: Sivan is a rocket scientist specializing in cryogenic propulsion and launch vehicle design. As ISRO chairman (2018–2022), he led Chandrayaan-2 and Chandrayaan-3, the latter achieving India's first soft landing near the Moon's south pole in 2023. He also oversaw the Gaganyaan human-spaceflight programme's early development. A Padma Shri recipient.

figures.name: Harish-Chandra
figures.tagline: Mathematician who revolutionized the representation theory of semisimple Lie groups — the Harish-Chandra theory.
figures.summary: Harish-Chandra was one of the most influential mathematicians of the 20th century. He developed the representation theory of semisimple Lie groups, introducing discrete series characters and the Harish-Chandra homomorphism. His work at the Institute for Advanced Study, Princeton, and the University of Chicago laid foundations used across modern mathematics and theoretical physics. A Fellow of the Royal Society.

figures.name: S. R. Srinivasa Varadhan
figures.tagline: Probabilist who won the Abel Prize for fundamental work on large deviations and diffusion processes.
figures.summary: Varadhan is a mathematician renowned for his work in probability theory, particularly large deviations theory and partial differential equations. The Varadhan formula and his contributions to diffusion processes are fundamental tools in stochastic analysis. He received the 2007 Abel Prize, often described as the Nobel of Mathematics, and the Padma Vibhushan. He is a professor at the Courant Institute, NYU.

figures.name: M. S. Narasimhan
figures.tagline: Geometer who founded the Tata Institute School of Mathematics and co-developed the Narasimhan–Seshadri theorem.
figures.summary: Narasimhan was an algebraic geometer who made foundational contributions to the theory of vector bundles on algebraic curves. With C. S. Seshadri he proved the Narasimhan–Seshadri theorem, linking stable bundles to unitary representations of fundamental groups — a landmark result with deep connections to physics. He founded the School of Mathematics at TIFR, Mumbai, and received the Padma Bhushan and Padma Vibhushan.

figures.name: C. S. Seshadri
figures.tagline: Algebraic geometer who founded the Chennai Mathematical Institute and co-proved the Narasimhan–Seshadri theorem.
figures.summary: Seshadri was a leading algebraic geometer whose work on vector bundles and moduli spaces transformed modern algebraic geometry. The Narasimhan–Seshadri theorem, proved with M. S. Narasimhan, is a foundational result bridging geometry and representation theory. He founded the Chennai Mathematical Institute and received the Padma Bhushan, the King Faisal Prize, and the Lerch Prize.

figures.name: Neena Gupta
figures.tagline: Commutative algebraist who solved the Zariski cancellation problem and won the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize.
figures.summary: Neena Gupta is a mathematician at the Indian Statistical Institute, Kolkata, known for her work in commutative algebra and algebraic geometry. She solved the Zariski cancellation problem for affine spaces over arbitrary fields, a long-standing open problem, and was awarded the 2021 Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Mathematical Sciences. She also received the 2024 DST-ICTP-IMU Ramanujan Prize.

figures.name: K. R. Parthasarathy
figures.tagline: Probabilist who founded quantum probability theory and quantum stochastic calculus.
figures.summary: Parthasarathy is a mathematician who pioneered quantum probability and quantum stochastic calculus, creating a framework that models quantum noise and underpins quantum information theory. A professor at ISI Delhi, he trained a generation of probabilists and received the Padma Shri and the Humboldt Research Award.

figures.name: Shreeram Shankar Abhyankar
figures.tagline: Algebraic geometer known for Abhyankar's lemma and resolving singularities in positive characteristic.
figures.summary: Abhyankar was a distinguished algebraic geometer whose work on resolution of singularities, local algebra, and algebraic curves earned international acclaim. Abhyankar's lemma is a standard tool in algebraic geometry. He taught at Purdue University for decades, supervised numerous doctoral students, and received the Padma Shri and the Steele Prize.

figures.name: T. R. Govindachari
figures.tagline: Natural-products chemist who pioneered research on Indian medicinal plants and alkaloids.
figures.summary: Govindachari was a chemist who advanced the chemistry of natural products in India, particularly alkaloids and terpenoids from Indian medicinal plants. He worked at the Central College, Bangalore, and the Indian Institute of Science, training generations of chemists. His research laid groundwork for phytochemistry and drug discovery from India's botanical wealth.

figures.name: Kamala Sohonie
figures.tagline: First Indian woman to earn a PhD in a scientific discipline — broke Cambridge's gender barrier to study nutrition.
figures.summary: Sohonie was a biochemist who became the first Indian woman to receive a PhD in a scientific discipline (Cambridge, 1939), after initially being denied admission to the Indian Institute of Science by C. V. Raman because she was a woman. Her thesis on the proteins of pulses contributed to understanding Indian nutrition. She later worked at the Royal Institute of Science, Mumbai, and on Neera (palm nectar) as a nutritional supplement.

figures.name: Pushpa Mittra Bhargava
figures.tagline: Father of Indian biotechnology — founded the Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB), Hyderabad.
figures.summary: Bhargava was a molecular biologist and the founding Director of CCMB, which he established in 1977 as India's premier centre for modern biology research. He championed biotechnology and genetic engineering in India and was an outspoken advocate for scientific temper and rationalism. A Padma Bhushan recipient, he remained an influential public intellectual until his death.

figures.name: Lalji Singh
figures.tagline: Father of Indian DNA fingerprinting — pioneered DNA-based identity testing and wildlife forensics in India.
figures.summary: Singh was a molecular biologist who developed and introduced DNA fingerprinting technology in India, with applications in paternity testing, criminal forensics, and wildlife conservation. He directed the Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology (CCMB) and later founded the Centre for DNA Fingerprinting and Diagnostics (CDFD), Hyderabad. A Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan recipient.

figures.name: Bidhan Chandra Roy
figures.tagline: Physician and second Chief Minister of West Bengal — National Doctors' Day in India marks his birth and death anniversary.
figures.summary: B. C. Roy was a renowned physician and educationist who established several medical institutions in Kolkata, including the Indian Medical Association and the Medical College Hospital. As Chief Minister of West Bengal (1948–1962) he advanced public health and education. India observes National Doctors' Day on 1 July, his birth and death anniversary, in his honour. He received the Bharat Ratna.

figures.name: E. Sreedharan
figures.tagline: The 'Metro Man' — built the Konkan Railway and Delhi Metro, transforming urban transport in India.
figures.summary: Sreedharan is a civil engineer credited with executing India's most challenging infrastructure projects on time. He led the Konkan Railway project through difficult terrain and later served as managing director of the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation, building India's first modern metro system. His reputation for integrity and project discipline earned him the Padma Shri and Padma Vibhushan.

figures.name: Brahm Prakash
figures.tagline: Metallurgist and founding director of BARC — advanced India's nuclear materials and alloy development.
figures.summary: Brahm Prakash was a metallurgical engineer who played a key role in establishing India's nuclear materials programme. As founding Director of the Metallurgy Division at BARC and later Director of IIT Kanpur, he advanced research on alloys, welding, and nuclear fuel materials. He helped build India's indigenous capability in strategic metallurgy.

figures.name: Vasant Ramji Gowariker
figures.tagline: Polymer scientist who developed polymers for India's rocket programme and advised on science policy.
figures.summary: Gowariker was a chemical engineer and polymer scientist who developed high-performance polymers used in Indian rocket and satellite applications. As Scientific Adviser to the Defence Minister and Secretary, Department of Defence R&D, he guided India's defence research and the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme. A Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan recipient.

figures.name: B. P. Pal
figures.tagline: Plant breeder and first Director General of ICAR — improved Indian wheat and rose varieties.
figures.summary: B. P. Pal was a geneticist and plant breeder who led agricultural research in India as Director General of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR). He developed improved wheat varieties and was renowned for his work on roses, writing the classic book 'The Rose in India'. He shaped India's post-independence agricultural research system.

figures.name: Dharmaraj Reddy
figures.tagline: Computer scientist who won the Turing Award for pioneering work in artificial intelligence and speech recognition.
figures.summary: Raj Reddy is a computer scientist whose work on large-scale AI systems, robotics, and speech recognition helped shape modern computing. He founded the Robotics Institute at Carnegie Mellon University and was a leading voice on using technology for social development. He received the 1994 Turing Award, the Padma Bhushan, and the Legion of Honour.

figures.name: M. S. Gopalakrishnan
figures.tagline: Algebraist who built the School of Mathematics at TIFR and advanced representation theory in India.
figures.summary: Gopalakrishnan was a mathematician whose research spanned algebra, representation theory, and number theory. He was instrumental in building the School of Mathematics at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research into a world-class centre and trained many Indian mathematicians. He received the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize.

figures.name: V. C. Kulkarni
figures.tagline: Commutative algebraist known for Kaplansky–Kulkarni results and teaching at IIT Bombay.
figures.summary: V. C. Kulkarni is a mathematician specializing in commutative algebra and ring theory. A long-time professor at IIT Bombay, he mentored generations of students and contributed to the development of mathematics education in India. He received the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Mathematical Sciences.

figures.name: S. Ramaseshan
figures.tagline: Physicist and director of IISc — advanced crystallography and materials science in India.
figures.summary: S. Ramaseshan was a physicist who made contributions to crystallography, X-ray diffraction, and materials science. As Director of the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore, he strengthened research and institution-building. He was the grandson of C. V. Raman's brother and carried forward a distinguished scientific lineage. A Padma Bhushan recipient.

figures.name: Ram Nath Chopra
figures.tagline: Father of Indian pharmacology — founded the Indian Research Fund Association and studied indigenous medicinal plants.
figures.summary: R. N. Chopra was a pharmacologist who established modern pharmacology in India. He founded the Indian Research Fund Association (precursor to ICMR) and conducted pioneering work on indigenous medicinal plants and their active compounds. His 'Glossary of Indian Medicinal Plants' remains a reference work.

figures.name: S. Ramanathan
figures.tagline: Organic chemist known for work on natural products and alkaloids; professor at IIT Madras.
figures.summary: S. Ramanathan was an organic chemist whose research focused on the chemistry of natural products, alkaloids, and terpenes. He taught at IIT Madras and the Indian Institute of Science, training generations of chemists. He received the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize and helped build India's organic chemistry research base.

figures.name: A. R. Krishnan
figures.tagline: Inorganic chemist and the first director of CSIR's Central Electrochemical Research Institute (CECRI), Karaikudi.
figures.summary: A. R. Krishnan was an inorganic chemist who founded CECRI and advanced electrochemical research in India, including work on batteries, corrosion, and metal finishing. He helped establish India's capabilities in electrochemistry and electrochemical technology for industry.

figures.name: Kariamanickam Srinivasa Krishnan
figures.tagline: Physicist who co-discovered the Raman effect with C. V. Raman and directed the National Physical Laboratory.
figures.summary: K. S. Krishnan was C. V. Raman's collaborator in the discovery of the Raman effect (1928), one of the most important discoveries in spectroscopy. He later directed the National Physical Laboratory, Delhi, and built India's capabilities in precision measurement and ultrasonics. A Fellow of the Royal Society and Padma Bhushan recipient.

figures.name: R. S. Mishra
figures.tagline: Metallurgist who advanced steel research and founded the National Metallurgical Laboratory's R&D programmes.
figures.summary: R. S. Mishra was a metallurgical engineer whose work on steelmaking, ironmaking, and materials processing supported India's industrial growth. He held leadership roles at CSIR's National Metallurgical Laboratory and contributed to national steel and materials research policy.

figures.name: A. P. Mitra
figures.tagline: Atmospheric physicist who founded the Indian programme in aeronomy and studied the upper atmosphere.
figures.summary: A. P. Mitra was a physicist who pioneered aeronomy — the study of Earth's upper atmosphere — in India. As Director of the National Physical Laboratory, he advanced research on atmospheric physics, radio wave propagation, and space science. He played a key role in establishing India's participation in international geophysical programmes.

figures.name: P. L. Dhingra
figures.tagline: Agricultural chemist who advanced soil science and fertilizer research in India.
figures.summary: P. L. Dhingra was an agricultural chemist whose work on soil fertility, plant nutrition, and fertilizers helped shape India's agricultural research. He worked at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute and contributed to the Green Revolution's scientific foundation.

figures.name: S. Varadarajan
figures.tagline: Mathematician known for work on Lie groups and harmonic analysis; professor at UCLA.
figures.summary: V. S. Varadarajan is a mathematician renowned for his work on Lie groups, their representations, and harmonic analysis, with applications to quantum mechanics. A professor at UCLA, he authored influential textbooks and trained many students. He received the Padma Shri and is a Fellow of the American Mathematical Society.

figures.name: M. R. Srinivasan
figures.tagline: Nuclear engineer who built India's nuclear power programme and chaired the Atomic Energy Commission.
figures.summary: M. R. Srinivasan was a nuclear engineer who played a central role in setting up India's nuclear power plants, including Tarapur and Madras Atomic Power Station. As Chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission (1987–1998), he guided India's nuclear energy programme and fast-breeder reactor development. A Padma Vibhushan recipient.

figures.name: H. K. Sen
figures.tagline: Chemical engineer and pioneer of membrane separation technology in India.
figures.summary: H. K. Sen was a chemical engineer whose research on membrane technology, separation processes, and biochemical engineering found applications in water treatment and biotechnology. He taught at the Indian Institute of Science and IIT Delhi and received the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize.

figures.name: R. C. Mehrotra
figures.tagline: Inorganic chemist known for organometallic chemistry and metal clusters; professor at IIT Kanpur.
figures.summary: R. C. Mehrotra was an inorganic chemist whose work on organometallic compounds, metal clusters, and coordination chemistry advanced the field in India. He taught at IIT Kanpur for decades, supervised numerous PhD students, and received the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Chemical Sciences.

figures.name: S. M. Mukherjee
figures.tagline: Physical chemist who advanced electrochemistry and founded research at Jadavpur University.
figures.summary: S. M. Mukherjee was a physical chemist known for his work on electrochemistry and chemical kinetics. He established strong research programmes at Jadavpur University, Kolkata, and mentored many chemists. He received the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize.

figures.name: K. C. Malhotra
figures.tagline: Plant pathologist who studied crop diseases and advanced agricultural plant protection in India.
figures.summary: K. C. Malhotra was a botanist and plant pathologist whose research on crop diseases, particularly fungal pathogens, helped Indian agriculture reduce yield losses. He worked at the Indian Agricultural Research Institute and contributed to plant protection science.

figures.name: V. R. Thadani
figures.tagline: Physicist who founded the physics department at the University of Delhi and taught generations.
figures.summary: V. R. Thadani was a physicist who helped establish the physics department at the University of Delhi and taught several generations of Indian physicists. His work spanned solid-state physics and science education.

figures.name: S. P. Chatterjee
figures.tagline: Statistician who founded the Institute of Statistical Studies and advanced statistics education in West Bengal.
figures.summary: S. P. Chatterjee was a statistician who played a key role in developing statistics education and research in West Bengal. He founded the Institute of Statistical Studies and contributed to the growth of the statistical profession in India.

figures.name: N. R. Sen
figures.tagline: Mathematician known for work on differential geometry and tensor analysis at the University of Calcutta.
figures.summary: N. R. Sen was a mathematician whose research on differential geometry and tensor analysis contributed to the mathematical foundations of relativity and geometry. He taught at the University of Calcutta and was a Fellow of several scientific academies.

figures.name: B. M. Udgaonkar
figures.tagline: Physicist who taught and popularized physics in western India at the Institute of Science, Mumbai.
figures.summary: B. M. Udgaonkar was a physicist and educationist at the Institute of Science, Mumbai, known for his clear teaching and contributions to physics education in Maharashtra. He trained many students who went on to lead Indian science.

figures.name: C. N. R. Rao
figures.tagline: Materials chemist and science adviser — one of India's most cited scientists, worked on nanomaterials.
figures.summary: C. N. R. Rao is a materials chemist whose research on solid-state and structural chemistry, nanomaterials, and hybrid materials has made him one of the most cited scientists from India. He served as scientific adviser to the Prime Minister, founded the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research (JNCASR), and received the Bharat Ratna and numerous international honours.

figures.name: G. K. Anklesaria
figures.tagline: Industrial chemist who advanced the chemical industry in Gujarat and founded research laboratories.
figures.summary: G. K. Anklesaria was an industrial chemist who contributed to the development of India's chemical and pharmaceutical industry, particularly in Gujarat. He founded research and testing laboratories and supported industrial chemistry education.

figures.name: N. S. Ramaswamy
figures.tagline: Biophysicist who developed image-processing methods for cryo-electron microscopy of macromolecules.
figures.summary: N. S. Ramaswamy is a molecular biophysicist known for developing computational methods to reconstruct three-dimensional structures of biological macromolecules from electron micrographs, foundational to modern cryo-EM. He worked at the Molecular Biophysics Unit, IISc Bangalore, and is a Fellow of the Royal Society.

figures.name: S. Bhagavantam
figures.tagline: Physicist who directed CSIR laboratories and advanced radio and cosmic-ray research in India.
figures.summary: S. Bhagavantam was a physicist whose work spanned radio physics, cosmic rays, and the ionosphere. He directed several CSIR laboratories and the Indian Institute of Technology, Kharagpur, and served as Vice-Chancellor of Osmania University. He helped build post-independence India's scientific infrastructure.

figures.name: K. N. Bahl
figures.tagline: Plant morphologist who advanced the study of Indian flora and taught at the University of Delhi.
figures.summary: K. N. Bahl was a botanist whose research on plant morphology and anatomy advanced the understanding of Indian plants. He taught at the University of Delhi and helped establish botany as a strong discipline in Indian universities.

figures.name: P. Maheshwari
figures.tagline: Embryologist who founded the modern study of plant embryology in India.
figures.summary: P. Maheshwari was a botanist who founded the modern study of plant embryology in India. His book 'An Introduction to the Embryology of Angiosperms' became a standard text worldwide. He taught at the University of Delhi and received the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize.

figures.name: M. S. Ramanathan
figures.tagline: Physicist who founded the physics department at Annamalai University and studied crystal physics.
figures.summary: M. S. Ramanathan was a physicist who established the physics department at Annamalai University and conducted research on crystal physics and ultrasonics. He trained many students and contributed to physics education in Tamil Nadu.

figures.name: K. S. Rajan
figures.tagline: Aerospace scientist who guided India's missile programmes and served as Scientific Adviser to the Defence Minister.
figures.summary: K. S. Rajan was an aerospace scientist who contributed to India's missile and aerospace programmes, including work on aerodynamics and launch vehicles. As Scientific Adviser to the Raksha Mantri and Director General of DRDO's aerospace cluster, he guided strategic technology development. A Padma Shri recipient.

figures.name: V. K. Saraswat
figures.tagline: Rocket scientist who led DRDO and the development of India's indigenous missile systems.
figures.summary: V. K. Saraswat is a rocket scientist who played a leading role in the development of India's Prithvi and Agni missile systems and served as Director General of DRDO and Scientific Adviser to the Defence Minister. He later joined NITI Aayog as a member overseeing science and technology. A Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan recipient.

figures.name: A. J. M. Salam
figures.tagline: Physicist who studied cosmic rays and high-energy physics at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research.
figures.summary: A. J. M. Salam was a physicist whose research on cosmic rays and high-energy physics contributed to TIFR's early experimental programme. He worked on balloon-borne and ground-based detectors and trained students in particle physics.

figures.name: D. S. Kothari
figures.tagline: Physicist and educationist — founded the University Grants Commission and shaped Indian higher education.
figures.summary: D. S. Kothari was a theoretical physicist whose research on the theory of the white dwarf and atmospheric electricity earned international recognition. He was the first Chairman of the University Grants Commission (UGC) and shaped India's higher-education system. The Kothari Commission on education bears his legacy. He received the Padma Bhushan and Padma Vibhushan.

figures.name: B. D. Nagchaudhuri
figures.tagline: Physicist who directed the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science and studied magnetism.
figures.summary: B. D. Nagchaudhuri was a physicist whose work on magnetism and solid-state physics advanced materials research in India. He directed the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science (IACS), Kolkata, and served as Vice-Chancellor of Jadavpur University.

figures.name: S. P. K. Gupta
figures.tagline: Physicist who advanced nuclear physics research and taught at the University of Delhi.
figures.summary: S. P. K. Gupta was a nuclear physicist who contributed to experimental nuclear physics and taught at the University of Delhi. He helped build India's nuclear research capabilities and trained students in the field.

figures.name: Aryabhata
figures.tagline: Pioneer of the place-value system and zero; author of the Aryabhatiya.
figures.summary: Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya (499 CE) laid foundations of Indian mathematics and astronomy, introducing the place-value system, algorithms for square and cube roots, and trigonometric sine tables. He correctly explained lunar and solar eclipses and estimated pi. His work remains taught in schools across India.

figures.name: Brahmagupta
figures.tagline: First to treat zero as a number and define rules for negative numbers.
figures.summary: In the Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE), Brahmagupta gave the first rules for arithmetic involving zero and negative numbers, solved quadratic equations, and worked on astronomy. His rules are still part of elementary mathematics.
figures.stillUsed: zero as a number and rules for negative numbers

figures.name: Bhaskara I
figures.tagline: Gave a remarkable rational approximation for the sine function.
figures.summary: Bhaskara I wrote commentary on Aryabhata and the Mahabhaskariya, providing a rational approximation for sine that is still noted for its accuracy. He advanced astronomy and algebra in the 7th century.

figures.name: Bhaskara II
figures.tagline: Author of Lilavati and Bijaganita; anticipated ideas of calculus.
figures.summary: Bhaskara II's Lilavati and Bijaganita cover arithmetic, algebra, and astronomy. He developed concepts resembling differential calculus and the derivative, and accurately determined the length of the year. His texts remain classics.

figures.name: Varahamihira
figures.tagline: Author of the Brihat Samhita; advanced astronomy and meteorology.
figures.summary: Varahamihira's Pancha Siddhantika and Brihat Samhita synthesized astronomy, meteorology, and natural science. He calculated planetary motions and explained comets and earthquakes. His astronomical tables were used for centuries.
figures.stillUsed: astronomical tables in the Brihat Samhita

figures.name: Kanada
figures.tagline: Founder of the Vaisheshika school; proposed atomism.
figures.summary: Kanada (also Kashyapa) founded the Vaisheshika school and proposed that matter is made of indivisible atoms (paramanus). His ideas prefigure atomic theory and remain part of India's intellectual heritage.

figures.name: Sushruta
figures.tagline: Author of the Sushruta Samhita; father of surgery.
figures.summary: Sushruta compiled the Sushruta Samhita, one of the earliest known texts on surgery and medicine. He described surgical procedures, instruments, and techniques such as rhinoplasty that are still studied in Ayurveda and surgical history.
figures.stillUsed: surgical techniques in the Sushruta Samhita

figures.name: Charaka
figures.tagline: Author of the Charaka Samhita; foundational Ayurvedic physician.
figures.summary: Charaka authored the Charaka Samhita, a foundational text of Ayurvedic medicine covering diagnosis, treatment, and preventive care. His principles of internal medicine continue to influence traditional Indian medicine.
figures.stillUsed: Ayurvedic principles in the Charaka Samhita

figures.name: Nagarjuna
figures.tagline: Pioneer of Indian chemistry and metallurgy; author of the Rasaratnakara.
figures.summary: Nagarjuna was associated with early Indian chemistry and metallurgy, working on the extraction and purification of metals and minerals. The Rasaratnakara tradition attributed to him influenced later alchemical and pharmaceutical practice.

figures.name: Pingala
figures.tagline: Author of the Chandahshastra; described binary numerals.
figures.summary: Pingala's Chandahshastra (2nd century BCE) presented a systematic study of Sanskrit prosody and described binary numerals in the form of laghu and guru syllables. His combinatorial ideas prefigure binary arithmetic.

figures.name: Aryabhata II
figures.tagline: Author of the Maha-Siddhanta; advanced algebra and astronomy.
figures.summary: Aryabhata II wrote the Maha-Siddhanta, advancing algebra, astronomy, and planetary calculations in the 10th century. His work on indeterminate equations and spherical astronomy built on earlier Indian traditions.
figures.stillUsed: astronomical and algebraic rules in the Maha-Siddhanta

figures.name: Lalla
figures.tagline: Astronomer who wrote the Sisyadhivriddida and described astronomical instruments.
figures.summary: Lalla was an 8th-century astronomer whose Sisyadhivriddida described planetary motions and astronomical instruments. He influenced later Islamic and Indian astronomical traditions.

figures.name: Sripati
figures.tagline: Mathematician and astronomer; wrote on astronomy and astrology.
figures.summary: Sripati was a 10th-century mathematician and astronomer who wrote on astronomy, astrology, and mathematics. His work contributed to the development of jyotisha and Indian computational astronomy.

figures.name: Manjula
figures.tagline: Astronomer who wrote a commentary on Aryabhata and the Laghu-manasa.
figures.summary: Manjula was a 10th-century astronomer who commented on Aryabhata's works and wrote the Laghu-manasa. His writings preserved and transmitted early Indian astronomical knowledge.

figures.name: Madhava of Sangamagrama
figures.tagline: Founder of the Kerala school; discovered infinite series for pi and trigonometric functions.
figures.summary: Madhava founded the Kerala school of astronomy and mathematics and discovered infinite series for pi, sine, and cosine centuries before similar results in Europe. His work laid foundations of calculus and analysis.
figures.stillUsed: Madhava's infinite series for pi and sine/cosine

figures.name: Nilakantha Somayaji
figures.tagline: Author of the Tantrasangraha; revised planetary models.
figures.summary: Nilakantha Somayaji was a leading astronomer of the Kerala school and author of the Tantrasangraha. He proposed a partially heliocentric planetary model and developed series expansions for planetary motions.
figures.stillUsed: Nilakantha's planetary models and series expansions

figures.name: Jyesthadeva
figures.tagline: Author of the Yuktibhasa, a calculus text of the Kerala school.
figures.summary: Jyesthadeva authored the Yuktibhasa in Malayalam, presenting rigorous derivations of the Kerala school's infinite series and calculus-like results. It is considered one of the earliest texts on calculus.

figures.name: Parameshvara
figures.tagline: Astronomer of the Kerala school; worked on eclipses and observations.
figures.summary: Parameshvara was a Kerala school astronomer who worked on eclipses, observational astronomy, and commentaries on earlier astronomers. He made careful observations of lunar and solar eclipses.

figures.name: Mahavira (mathematician)
figures.tagline: Author of the Ganita-sara-sangraha; advanced arithmetic and algebra.
figures.summary: Mahavira was a 9th-century mathematician who authored the Ganita-sara-sangraha, covering arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and mensuration. His rules for arithmetic operations were widely used in India.

figures.name: Sridhara
figures.tagline: Mathematician who wrote on algebra and quadratic equations.
figures.summary: Sridhara was a 9th–10th century mathematician known for his work on algebra, including methods for solving quadratic equations. His texts influenced later Indian mathematical education.

figures.name: Mahendra Suri
figures.tagline: Astronomer who wrote the Yantra-raja on astronomical instruments.
figures.summary: Mahendra Suri was a 14th-century astronomer at the court of Firuz Shah Tughlaq and wrote the Yantra-raja, a treatise on the astrolabe and other astronomical instruments.
figures.stillUsed: designs for the Yantra-raja astronomical instrument

figures.name: Sisir Kumar Mitra
figures.tagline: Pioneered ionospheric and radio research in India.
figures.summary: Sisir Kumar Mitra was a physicist who pioneered research on the ionosphere and radio waves in India. He established the ionospheric field in India and wrote the influential book 'The Upper Atmosphere'.

figures.name: P. R. Pisharoty
figures.tagline: Father of remote sensing in India; meteorologist and physicist.
figures.summary: P. R. Pisharoty was a meteorologist and physicist considered the father of remote sensing in India. He worked with Vikram Sarabhai and helped establish India's space-based meteorology and remote sensing programmes.
figures.stillUsed: remote sensing techniques in Indian meteorology

figures.name: K. R. Ramanathan
figures.tagline: Meteorologist who studied the ozone layer and atmospheric physics.
figures.summary: K. R. Ramanathan was an eminent meteorologist who directed the India Meteorological Department and studied atmospheric physics, solar radiation, and the ozone layer. He was president of the International Union of Geodesy and Geophysics.

figures.name: D. N. Wadia
figures.tagline: Pioneering geologist who mapped the geology of the Himalaya.
figures.summary: D. N. Wadia was a pioneering Indian geologist who mapped the geology of the Himalaya and established modern geological research in India. He wrote 'Geology of India' and founded the Indian Bureau of Petroleum.

figures.name: S. R. Ranganathan
figures.tagline: Father of library science in India; created the colon classification system.
figures.summary: S. R. Ranganathan was a librarian and mathematician who founded modern library science in India. He created the Colon Classification system and the Five Laws of Library Science, still used in libraries worldwide.

figures.name: B. C. Guha
figures.tagline: Physical anthropologist who studied the peoples of India.
figures.summary: B. C. Guha was a physical anthropologist who conducted pioneering anthropometric surveys of the peoples of India. He founded the Anthropological Survey of India and advanced the study of human variation.

figures.name: M. Annadurai
figures.tagline: ISRO's 'Moon Man' who directed the Chandrayaan-1 lunar mission.
figures.summary: M. Annadurai is an ISRO scientist who served as project director of Chandrayaan-1, India's first lunar mission, which confirmed water molecules on the Moon. He later led the Mars Orbiter Mission and Chandrayaan-2 programmes and directed the U R Rao Satellite Centre.
figures.stillUsed: India's lunar and Mars mission programme

figures.name: S. Somanath
figures.tagline: ISRO chairman who led Chandrayaan-3 to the Moon's south pole.
figures.summary: S. Somanath is a rocket scientist and ISRO chairman who oversaw Chandrayaan-3, which achieved India's first soft landing near the lunar south pole in 2023. He has played a key role in the development of India's launch vehicles and the Gaganyaan human-spaceflight programme.
figures.stillUsed: India's launch vehicle and lunar programme

figures.name: S. K. Shivakumar
figures.tagline: ISRO scientist who led telemetry, tracking and command for interplanetary missions.
figures.summary: S. K. Shivakumar is an ISRO scientist known for his work on spacecraft telemetry, tracking, and command. He played a central role in the Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) and Chandrayaan missions, ensuring communication with distant spacecraft.

figures.name: T. K. Alex
figures.tagline: ISRO satellite director who advanced India's remote-sensing and navigation satellites.
figures.summary: T. K. Alex is an ISRO scientist who served as director of the ISRO Satellite Centre, overseeing the development of India's remote-sensing, communication, and navigation satellites including the IRNSS/NavIC constellation.
figures.stillUsed: India's satellite and NavIC navigation programme

figures.name: G. Satheesh Reddy
figures.tagline: Aerospace scientist who led DRDO as chairman and advanced indigenous missile systems.
figures.summary: G. Satheesh Reddy is an aerospace scientist who served as Chairman of DRDO and Scientific Adviser to the Defence Minister. He guided the development of India's indigenous missile systems, including Astra, Akash, and the Quick Reaction Surface-to-Air Missile.
figures.stillUsed: India's indigenous missile and defence technology

figures.name: Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar
figures.tagline: Father of research laboratories in India; founder-director of CSIR.
figures.summary: Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar was a chemist who founded a network of national research laboratories and served as the first director-general of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR). The Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize, India's top science award, is named in his honour.

figures.name: M. S. Raghunathan
figures.tagline: Mathematician known for work on lattices in Lie groups; director of IIT Bombay.
figures.summary: M. S. Raghunathan is a mathematician renowned for his work on discrete subgroups of Lie groups and the Raghunathan theorem. He served as director of IIT Bombay and helped build India's advanced mathematics research ecosystem.
figures.stillUsed: Raghunathan theorem on lattices in Lie groups

figures.name: R. Parimala
figures.tagline: Algebraic geometer known for work on quadratic forms and the Serre conjecture.
figures.summary: R. Parimala is an algebraic geometer whose work on quadratic forms over function fields and the Serre conjecture (now a theorem) has had wide influence. She is a professor at Emory University and a fellow of several scientific academies.
figures.stillUsed: results on quadratic forms over function fields

figures.name: Homi N. Sethna
figures.tagline: Nuclear engineer and chairman of India's Atomic Energy Commission.
figures.summary: Homi N. Sethna was a nuclear engineer who played a central role in India's nuclear energy programme. As chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission (1973–1983), he oversaw India's first peaceful nuclear explosion and the expansion of nuclear power.
figures.stillUsed: India's nuclear power and materials programme

figures.name: R. Chidambaram
figures.tagline: Nuclear physicist who was a key figure in India's nuclear programme.
figures.summary: R. Chidambaram was a nuclear physicist and principal scientific adviser to the Government of India. He played a leading role in India's nuclear tests of 1974 and 1998 and shaped the country's nuclear and materials science policy.
figures.stillUsed: India's nuclear programme and science policy

figures.name: P. K. Iyengar
figures.tagline: Nuclear engineer and chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission.
figures.summary: P. K. Iyengar was a nuclear engineer who served as chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission and director of BARC. He contributed to India's nuclear power programme and the development of nuclear reactors and fuel cycle technology.

figures.name: V. Rajaraman
figures.tagline: Pioneer of computer science education in India; author of early programming textbooks.
figures.summary: V. Rajaraman is a computer scientist who pioneered computer science education in India at IIT Kanpur and the Indian Institute of Science. He authored influential textbooks on programming and numerical methods and helped establish computing in Indian institutions.
figures.stillUsed: computer science curricula in Indian institutions

figures.name: B. M. Johri
figures.tagline: Embryologist and morphologist who advanced plant embryology in India.
figures.summary: B. M. Johri was a botanist whose research on plant embryology and morphology advanced the understanding of plant development. He taught at the University of Delhi and mentored generations of plant scientists.

figures.name: K. S. Valdiya
figures.tagline: Geologist who studied the Himalaya and neotectonics of India.
figures.summary: K. S. Valdiya is a geologist known for his work on the geology and neotectonics of the Himalaya and the Indian subcontinent. He has written extensively on the evolution of the Himalaya and natural hazards.

figures.name: M. S. Thiagarajan
figures.tagline: Inorganic chemist known for work on bioinorganic chemistry and metal complexes.
figures.summary: M. S. Thiagarajan is an inorganic chemist whose research on bioinorganic chemistry and metal complexes has applications in medicine and catalysis. He taught at IIT Madras and received the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize.

figures.name: G. S. Pandey
figures.tagline: Physicist who advanced liquid crystal and materials research in India.
figures.summary: G. S. Pandey is a physicist known for his work on liquid crystals and soft condensed matter. He has taught at Banaras Hindu University and contributed to the development of materials physics in India.

figures.name: S. G. Dani
figures.tagline: Mathematician known for work on ergodic theory and dynamical systems.
figures.summary: S. G. Dani is a mathematician whose research on ergodic theory, homogeneous dynamics, and Diophantine approximation has had wide influence. He taught at the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay.
figures.stillUsed: ergodic theory and dynamical systems methods

figures.name: J. K. Verma
figures.tagline: Mathematician known for work on commutative algebra and homological algebra.
figures.summary: J. K. Verma is a mathematician whose research on commutative algebra and homological algebra has advanced the field. He taught at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay and trained many students.

figures.name: V. S. Sunder
figures.tagline: Mathematician known for work on operator algebras and von Neumann algebras.
figures.summary: V. S. Sunder is a mathematician whose research on operator algebras and von Neumann algebras has contributed to functional analysis. He taught at the Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Chennai, and the Indian Statistical Institute.

figures.name: M. R. Srinivasan
figures.tagline: Nuclear engineer who built India's nuclear power programme and chaired the Atomic Energy Commission.
figures.summary: M. R. Srinivasan was a nuclear engineer who played a central role in setting up India's nuclear power plants, including Tarapur and Madras Atomic Power Station. As Chairman of the Atomic Energy Commission (1987–1998), he guided India's nuclear energy programme and fast-breeder reactor development. A Padma Vibhushan recipient.
figures.stillUsed: India's nuclear power and fast-breeder reactor programme

figures.name: V. K. Saraswat
figures.tagline: Rocket scientist who led DRDO and the development of India's indigenous missile systems.
figures.summary: V. K. Saraswat is a rocket scientist who played a leading role in the development of India's Prithvi and Agni missile systems and served as Director General of DRDO and Scientific Adviser to the Defence Minister. He later joined NITI Aayog as a member overseeing science and technology. A Padma Shri and Padma Bhushan recipient.
